<div class="course-section-head" id="course-curiosities"><h2>Explore further</h2></div>

<div class="course-curiosities">
<details>
<summary>Conservation can simplify the equations</summary>

In a reversible reaction $A \rightleftharpoons B$, at constant volume, with no inflow or outflow and a one-to-one conversion, the total concentration $a(t)+b(t)$ is constant.

This lets us express one variable in terms of the other and reduce the number of independent equations. Before solving, look for conserved quantities.

<p class="curiosity-link"><a href="chemical-modeling.html">Read the chemical-reactions note →</a></p>
</details>

<details>
<summary>Why does a second-order equation need two initial conditions?</summary>

For an equation $x^{\prime\prime}=f(t,x,x^\prime)$, set $v=x^\prime$ to obtain $x^\prime=v$, $v^\prime=f(t,x,v)$. The state contains **position and velocity**.

For the pendulum, the initial angle alone is insufficient: different initial velocities give different motions. Under the usual existence and uniqueness conditions, both data determine the local solution.

<p class="curiosity-link"><a href="second-order.html">See the transformation step by step →</a></p>
</details>

<details>
<summary>The same pendulum, two descriptions</summary>

The ideal model uses $\sin\theta$. Near the downward vertical, $\sin\theta\approx\theta$ when the angle is measured in radians. This yields a useful linear model for small oscillations.

At larger amplitudes, the approximation loses accuracy. The phase plane helps compare trajectories and identify when the nonlinear model is needed.

<p class="curiosity-link"><a href="phase-plane.html">Study the pendulum in the phase plane →</a></p>
</details>

</div>
